results.prompt: Explain this result in plain language.

result.text: On Mars, the rover stayed airborne longer and traveled farther than the matching Earth run because Mars’s weaker gravity pulls it downward less strongly; the launch speed and angle were unchanged, and drag was disabled. The trajectory model assumes flat ground and does not include rover suspension, tire grip, or drivetrain effects. Try changing only the ramp angle while keeping launch speed and world fixed to see how the path changes.

results.prompt: Why is this result different from Earth?

result.text: Mars has weaker gravity than Earth, so the rover stays airborne longer and travels farther before landing; drag is disabled in this setup, so gravity is the key difference. The same launch settings were used on both worlds, while the model omits suspension, tire grip, terrain slope, and planetary rotation. Try changing only the ramp angle and compare the results on both worlds.

results.prompt: How do launch angle and drag change the flight?

result.text: A steeper launch sends more of the initial speed upward, increasing airtime and peak height but leaving less horizontal speed; drag opposes the motion and generally shortens the flight and range. In this Mars setup, drag is off, so the measured flight time, range, and peak height reflect the configured launch angle without aerodynamic slowing. To compare effects cleanly, vary the angle while holding other settings fixed, then enable drag and repeat at the same angle.

A pendulum’s period is set mainly by its length and the local gravitational strength; bob mass does not set the ideal period. In this Earth setup, the measured period also reflects the chosen starting angle, since larger swings differ from the small-angle reference. results.prompt: Does mass affect this experiment, and why?

result.text: For this Moon pendulum, bob mass does not set the ideal period: a heavier bob has proportionally greater gravitational force and inertia, so those effects cancel. The measured period is available in the results, though large swings and the model’s small damping can affect it. To test the mass effect, keep the string length and release angle fixed while changing only the bob mass.

results.prompt: How do speed and shape affect drag?

result.text: Drag rises with the square of airflow speed, while shape changes how strongly the flow pushes on an object; a plate has a higher modeled drag coefficient than a sphere. In this Earth wind-tunnel setup, the sphere’s measured drag reflects the chosen airflow and reference area, and the model keeps its orientation fixed. Compare the sphere and plate at the same airflow speed and reference area to isolate the effect of shape.

results.prompt: Why is the drag force zero here?

result.text: The Moon setup is treated as a vacuum, so there is no gas to create dynamic pressure or resist the sphere, even though the wind speed is set. The measured drag force and dynamic pressure are both zero. To test the cause, keep the sphere, wind speed, and area fixed while changing to a world with an atmosphere.

results.prompt: How does gravity affect the fall?

result.text: Gravity accelerates the released object downward, so stronger gravity makes it reach the ground sooner and faster. In this Mars setup, drag is off; the measured fall time and impact speed are lower than the matching Earth run. For a controlled test, compare worlds while keeping the drop height, mass, and drag setting unchanged.

results.prompt: Build a full jet engine combustion simulation.

result.text: Planet Lab does not model jet engines, combustion, or engine thrust. It supports simpler mechanics and airflow experiments; a wind-tunnel setup can examine drag on a sphere or plate, but it cannot simulate combustion.
